title: Debt II: convertible bonds and accrued interest

reading.h: The convertible bond and its conversion ratio
reading.body:
A **convertible bond** lets the holder exchange it for a fixed number of the issuer's common shares. The terms are set at issue as either a **conversion price (CP)** or a **conversion ratio (CR)**. Each one defines the other:

**CR = Par ÷ CP** and **CP = Par ÷ CR.**

With $1,000 par and a conversion price of $25, the ratio is 1,000 ÷ 25 = **40 shares**. Think of the bond as redeemable for 40 shares of stock. Everything else, parity and arbitrage, just asks whether those 40 shares are worth more or less than the bond's price. Compute the ratio first, every time. The coupon and current yield in the stem are distractors.

reading.h: Parity — the exchange rate, both directions
reading.body:
**Parity** is the price at which the bond and the shares it converts into are worth exactly the same. There are two forms, and the exam asks both.

**Parity price of the STOCK = bond price ÷ CR.** That is what you pay per share by buying the bond and converting. A bond at $1,080 with CR 40 gives 1,080 ÷ 40 = **$27** per share.

**Parity price of the BOND = stock price × CR.** That is what the bond is worth if converted right now. Stock at $28 with CR 40 gives 28 × 40 = **$1,120**.

Same ratio. Multiply one way to get a share price. Divide the other way to get a bond price. Read the question to see which side it wants.

reading.h: Arbitrage: is the bond cheaper than its shares?
reading.body:
Arbitrage exists only when the bond trades **below** parity, meaning the shares it converts into are worth more than the bond costs. Then you **buy the bond, convert to shares, and sell the shares** for the difference.

Take a bond at $1,080, CR 40, stock at $28. Parity price of the bond = 28 × 40 = $1,120. The bond at $1,080 is **below** parity of $1,120. So buy the bond for $1,080, convert to 40 shares, and sell them at $28 for $1,120, a **$40 profit** per bond before commissions. If the bond traded **at or above** $1,120, there would be no arbitrage. The whole test is whether the shares are worth more than the bond price.

reading.h: Anti-dilution, and why conversion isn't taxable
reading.body:
A stock split or stock dividend would dilute the convertible holder, so the terms **adjust automatically**. The CR rises and the CP falls to keep the holder's economics unchanged. A 2-for-1 split turns CP $25 into **$12.50** and CR 40 into **80**. A 25% stock dividend multiplies CR by 1.25 and divides CP by 1.25.

**Converting** a bond into stock is **not a taxable event**. You swap one security for another; you do not sell. The stock inherits the bond's cost basis (bond basis ÷ shares received). Issuers like convertibles because the option lets them pay a **lower** coupon. A rising stock also lets them force conversion by calling the bond when it trades well above the call price.

reading.h: Accrued interest: the buyer pays the seller
reading.body:
Bonds pay interest **in arrears**, a lump sum on each coupon date. So when a bond trades between coupon dates, the **buyer pays the seller** the interest earned since the last coupon. It is added to the price on the confirmation. The buyer gets it back later by collecting the **full** next coupon.

Interest accrues from the **last coupon date up to, but NOT including, the settlement date**. The seller owns every night they held it. The buyer starts owning on settlement night. Some bonds trade **flat**, with no accrued interest at all: **zero-coupon, income/adjustment, and defaulted** bonds, plus any trade that settles exactly on a coupon date.

reading.h: Counting the days: 30/360 vs actual, under T+1
reading.body:
First find **settlement**. Regular way is **T+1**, one business day after the trade, skipping weekends and holidays. Then count from the last coupon to settlement with the right calendar. **Corporate and municipal bonds** use **30/360**: every month is 30 days, the year is 360, and February has 30 days. **U.S. Treasuries** use **actual days**; the exam uses actual/365.

Worked corporate example: an 8% bond pays Jan 15 and Jul 15, bought Tuesday **Mar 10, 2026**, settles Wednesday **Mar 11**. Count 30/360 from Jan 15 up to but not including Mar 11: 16 (Jan) + 30 (Feb) + 10 (Mar) = **56 days**. AI = $80 × 56/360 = **$12.44**. The same trade as a **Treasury** uses actual days: Feb 15 to 28 = 14, Mar 1 to 10 = 10, for **24 days**. Traps: counting the settlement date, using the trade date, or applying 30/360 to a Treasury.

flashcards.back: CR = Par ÷ CP. $1,000 par, CP $25 → 40 shares. (And CP = Par ÷ CR.)
Only when the bond trades BELOW parity. Buy the bond, convert, sell the shares for the difference.
Bond $1,080, CR 40, stock $28: parity bond = $1,120; profit = $1,120 − $1,080 = $40/bond.
CR doubles (40→80), CP halves ($25→$12.50). Holder's economics unchanged.

flashcards.front: Is converting a bond to stock taxable?
flashcards.back: No, not a taxable event. Stock inherits the bond's cost basis (bond basis ÷ shares).

flashcards.front: Who pays accrued interest, and to whom?
flashcards.back: The buyer pays the seller the interest earned since the last coupon. The buyer gets it back through the full next coupon.
From the last coupon date up to, but NOT including, the settlement date.
Zero-coupon, income/adjustment, and defaulted bonds; also trades settling on a coupon date.
Corporate & muni = 30/360 (Feb = 30 days). Treasury = actual days (exam: actual/365).
T+1: one business day after the trade, skipping weekends and holidays.

quiz.stem: A convertible bond has a par value of $1,000 and a conversion price of $50. What is its conversion ratio?
quiz.explanation: CR = par ÷ conversion price = $1,000 ÷ $50 = 20 shares. Dividing the other way ($50/$1,000) or reusing the $25/40-share example are the traps.

quiz.stem: A $1,000 par convertible bond is convertible into 40 shares of common stock, which is currently trading at $30. The parity price of the bond is:
quiz.explanation: Parity price of the bond = stock price × CR = $30 × 40 = $1,200. $750 divides instead of multiplies (that would be a share-side calculation), and $1,000 is just par.

quiz.stem: A 5% convertible bond with a conversion price of $25 is trading at $1,080. The common stock trades at $28. What arbitrage profit per bond, before commissions, is available?
options: None, because the bond trades above parity
quiz.explanation: CR = $1,000 ÷ $25 = 40; parity price of the bond = $28 × 40 = $1,120. The bond at $1,080 is below parity, so buy it, convert, and sell 40 shares at $28 for $1,120 — a $40 profit. The 5% coupon is a distractor.

quiz.stem: An 8% corporate bond pays interest on January 15 and July 15. A customer buys one $1,000 bond on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, regular way. How much accrued interest does the buyer pay the seller?
quiz.explanation: Regular way is T+1, so settlement is Wednesday March 11. Using 30/360, count Jan 15 up to but not including Mar 11: 16 + 30 + 10 = 56 days; $80 × 56/360 = $12.44. $12.67 wrongly includes the settlement date (57 days); $12.22 uses 55.

quiz.stem: A 4% Treasury note pays interest on February 15 and August 15. A customer buys the note on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, regular way. How many days of accrued interest will the buyer pay?
quiz.explanation: Treasuries settle T+1 (Wednesday March 11) and accrue on actual calendar days up to but not including settlement: Feb 15–28 = 14, plus Mar 1–10 = 10, for 24 days. 26 wrongly applies corporate 30/360 to a Treasury; 25 and 27 include the settlement date.

quiz.stem: Which of the following bonds trades FLAT (without accrued interest)?
options: A 6% corporate debenture between coupon dates
A 4% Treasury note between coupon dates
quiz.explanation: Zero-coupon bonds pay no periodic interest, so there is nothing to accrue — they trade flat, as do income/adjustment and defaulted bonds. Ordinary interest-paying corporates, Treasuries, and munis all trade with accrued interest between coupon dates.

quiz.stem: A customer converts a convertible bond into common stock. For tax purposes, this conversion is:
options: A taxable sale, with gain measured against the bond's cost
Not a taxable event; the stock takes the bond's cost basis
Taxable only if the stock is later sold at a loss
Taxable as ordinary income equal to the parity value
quiz.explanation: Exchanging a convertible for the underlying stock is not a taxable event — the stock simply inherits the bond's cost basis, and tax is deferred until the shares are sold. Treating conversion itself as a sale is the trap.

quiz.stem: A convertible bond has a conversion ratio of 40. The issuer declares a 2-for-1 stock split. After the anti-dilution adjustment, the conversion ratio and conversion price become:
quiz.explanation: A 2-for-1 split doubles the shares, so the CR doubles to 80 and the CP halves from $25 to $12.50, leaving the holder's economic position unchanged. Leaving the terms unchanged, or lowering the CR, would dilute the holder — both traps.
